segments.caption: The gambler's fallacy.
A true story from a casino, the simple maths, a million-flip test, and how it fools you every day. Save this one!
You flip a fair coin five times. Heads, heads, heads, heads, heads.
What's the next flip more likely to be? Heads, tails, or 50-50? Comment your answer before I tell you.
Monte Carlo, 1913. At the roulette table, the ball lands on black. Again. And again.
After 10 blacks, the crowd is sure red is due. They bet more and more on red.
Black came up 26 times in a row. The gamblers lost millions. The casino won.
So, the coin. The answer is 50-50. Still.
A coin has no memory. It doesn't know what happened before. Each flip is a brand new event.
Statisticians call this independence: the past flips don't change the next one.
So why does tails feel due? Because five heads in a row feels rare. And it is: 1 in 32.
But that was before you started. Once those five heads have happened, they're history. The only question left is one flip: half, half.
Your brain expects small samples to look balanced. The law of large numbers only works over thousands of flips, not five.
Don't trust me? We flipped a coin one million times on a computer.
5 heads in a row happened 31,000 times. And the very next flip? Heads exactly 50% of the time.
And Monte Carlo? 26 in a row is about 1 in 66 million. Incredibly rare.
But even after 25 blacks, the next spin was still the same 48.6% for black. Rare streaks happen. They just don't change the odds.
It fools us everywhere.
A couple with three boys thinks the fourth must be a girl. It's still about 50-50.
A captain who lost five tosses thinks he's due to win the next one. The coin doesn't care.
And people avoid last week's lottery numbers. They're exactly as likely as any others.
And watch out for the opposite mistake too: thinking heads is hot, so heads will continue. That's also wrong for a fair coin.
But careful: this only applies to truly random, independent events. A batter in form, or a slot machine that's rigged? Different story.
So remember: random events have no memory. The past doesn't make anything due.
Save this, and send it to the friend who says "this time I'm due."
